did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 20 begins with the response of Zophar the Naamathite, who replies to Job and presents his view of the fate of the wicked.
Did you know? Zophar argues that the joy of the hypocrite and the wicked is nothing new, but brief and fleeting—a truth known since ancient times.
Did you know? Even if the wicked exalt themselves to the heavens and reach the clouds with their heads, Zophar says their greatness will not last.
Did you know? The disappearance of the wicked is described in striking images: they will vanish like their own dung, and those who once saw them will later ask, “Where are they?”
Did you know? Zophar compares the fate of the wicked to a dream or a vision of the night—something seen for a moment, then gone without a trace.
Did you know? Evil is described as sweet in the mouth of the wicked, but later it turns bitter within them and becomes poison.
Did you know? The wealth the wicked have “swallowed” will not remain theirs: according to Zophar, God will make them vomit it up and expel it from their bodies.
Did you know? Zophar says the wicked will not enjoy rivers of honey and cream—symbols of abundance, sweetness, and blessing.
Did you know? According to Zophar, the root of the wicked person’s troubles is oppressing the poor and seizing homes; therefore, even when he amasses wealth, he finds no peace.
Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the heavens and the earth themselves are portrayed as exposing and rising against the wicked person’s wrongdoing—and this is the portion God assigns him.
